content.thinking:
I'll plan to verify with typecheck and preview after writing, then start setting up the module imports and builder structure for the treasure hoard scene.

I'm defining a simple transform class to handle positions, rotations, and parent-child hierarchies for placing objects in world space, building up world points, directions, and quaternions from local Euler angles.

Writing part placement helper...

I'm confirming the Euler order typing works with the spread tuple, and noting glow only applies to flat-colored parts since painted fills with flat:true should still work fine. I'm also considering whether part names need to be unique or if auto-naming handles duplicates, and cataloging the available geometry helpers (box, cylinder, cone, sphere, octahedron, icosahedron, torus, lathe) plus a merge/bake utility for combining transformed geometries.

I'm grouping geometries by color into batches, converting them to non-indexed form, merging each color group, then creating a single part per color with flat shading so normals come out faceted correctly. Now I'm defining the gold color palette with highlight, mid, dark, and deep tones.

Still filling in colors...

Adding a few more color variants brings the flat palette to about 22 colors, which feels right. Now I'm defining the painted gold material with mottled texture and orange-brown shadow tones for the chest bands, crown, goblets, and trim, then working out texel density for those painted areas.

Next I'm setting up dark gold, silver, and wood grain paint variants, with the wood grain oriented along the chest's horizontal plank direction using its local axis for the seams.

I should limit the seam lines to side faces rather than top faces, gating by |n.y|<0.5. Then for the crimson velvet, I'm setting up a diamond pattern paint function that picks two coordinates based on the surface normal and draws highlight lines where their rotated sum/difference is near zero.

Writing lattice line logic...

Now shifting to SVG textures, starting with a gold coin face emblem with a dark outer ring.

I'm mapping out the rune band texture for the chest rim strip, adjusting its viewBox aspect ratio to match the stretched proportions and rendering it on a plane rather than a box face. Then I'm planning the sparkle asset as a glowing four-point star with cyan/pink tint, and starting on a hextech glow effect texture.

For the goblet, I'm deciding to skip texturing the lathe geometry directly and instead wrap a thin cylindrical band with the rune texture around the bowl, checking that the aspect ratio of texture to circumference lines up well.

I can reuse this same band approach for the chest, and reuse the coin face texture at a smaller scale for the ingot stamp rather than designing a new one. Tallying up what's needed now: coin face, chest emblem, rune band, sparkle, tassel, plus a small ingot crest variant and a scroll band.

I'm also adding a glowing cyan hextech lock texture for the lock plate, bringing the count to seven. Now I'm laying out the chest's frame and dimensions, placing the main body box with painted wood fill, then adding an inner dark top panel and rim boards.

Still placing trim and structural pieces...

For the extrusion direction, outline runs along x with y up, giving thickness pointing forward in z. I'll add an emblem texture plane on the front face with a shield-and-wings design and a glowing hex lock on top, cut with alpha transparency so the gold wings read against the wood background rather than a solid plate.

Now I'm setting up the lid: a frame transform positioned at the back edge, rotated open around x, with the lid itself defined as an arch shape extruded along the width axis, depth mapped to local z and height along local y so the curve reads correctly once placed.

For the lid, I'm planning separate materials: the arch wood piece uses a mottled grain oriented along the chest's x-axis rather than the regular plank seams, since the lid's rotation would make horizontal seams look wrong. I'm also adding gold rib bands as slightly larger extrusions following the same arch shape to decorate the lid.

Now I'm placing the interior lining as a crimson box recessed below the rim, with a thin gold border frame of four strips around its edges to finish the inside trim.

Adding studs and hinge details...

Working out the rotation so the medallion face orients correctly: with a 90° rotation about X, the plane's top edge points toward the front of the lid, which stays upright once the lid opens to 100°. The chest interior holds coin lumps, gems, a goblet, and loose jewels piled inside, with a few gems resting on top. Now I'm placing a crown on a cushion positioned near the front of the chest.

Working out the cushion's position and tilt on the right heap, then placing the crown on top with its own size and offset. For the cushion geometry, I'm computing the local axis directions via cross products to get the thickness direction pointing upward, then outlining a rounded rectangle with beveled edges for the extrusion.

For finishing touches, I'm adding a gold cord sweep around the cushion's edge using the outline points, plus small gold bead tassels at each of the four corners with hanging card elements.

Now I'm working out the crown geometry sitting on the cushion, building a lathed or sphere-based dome shape for the velvet cap inside the gold ring.

Still writing lathe profile...

Still shaping spike geometry...

For gem orientation I need to rotate each gem so its axis points radially outward, using an aim-style quaternion that maps +Y to the target direction, with a direct world-space dir override for placement. Then I'm planning arches crossing over the top, using a spline from the band at radius 0.17 up to an apex point.

Four arches at 90-degree intervals meet at the apex, swept with a hexagonal cross-section in gold paint, topped with a small glowing crystal (cyan octahedron stretched for a Hextech feel). I'm also adding gold stud decorations along the base ring of the band.

Now I'm sketching the goblet structure: a function that builds a lathed solid using a profile curve, with tilt, scale, paint and gem color options, starting with the foot's outline points.

Checking that the outline closes properly along the axis without the inner and outer wall points crossing each other.

For the goblet interior, I'm considering adding a fill like coins or gems using a flattened sphere shape to suggest treasure inside the bowl.

Each goblet will get a distinct fill: one heaped with gems, one with a coin stack, one tipped over spilling coins, and one with a glowing cyan jeweled liquid disc. I'll apply gold and silver paint materials for the lathe shapes and add a rune-textured gem band around the bowl using a truncated cone matching the bowl's radius profile.

I'm also adding a small ring of gems at the stem knop, and I'll skip the foot-rim pearls and handles since this is a chalice design.

For the larger silver trophy goblet, I'll add two scrolled handles with a swept arc shape from the bowl midpoint outward and down, while deciding placement for the gold gem-filled goblet somewhere on the floor or atop the coin spill.

Rather than manually computing lump heights at specific coordinates, I think it's cleaner to write a reusable heightAt(x,z) function that sums contributions from each coin-pile lump using an ellipsoid falloff formula, then set each goblet's base to sink slightly below that computed surface height. This way goblets settle naturally into the coin piles regardless of their position, even accounting for yaw-rotated lumps.

Now I'm placing the three goblets: a tall gold one on the left heap, a large silver trophy with handles on the right, and a toppled gold goblet lying on its side near the front-center spilling coins outward, working out its tilt axis and resting height on the floor.

Then I add a fourth small gold goblet with glowing cyan liquid behind the left heap, and move on to defining gem geometry, starting with a brilliant-cut lathe profile for the pavilion shape.

Writing lathe profiles...

Then I'm sizing hero gems between 0.09–0.12 and placing them on the heap using the heightAt function to sit correctly on the pile surface.

I'm also planning scatter gems: roughly 7 large gems in six colors plus 18 small ones distributed across the heap surface, merged by color for efficient rendering, then applying glow at reduced strength around 0.45 so the emissive boost brightens colors without flattening out the facet shading entirely.

Now I'm designing the hextech crystal cluster for the back-left area: five cyan hex prisms at varying tilts, with smaller magenta accents, built using a lathe profile with tapered points to form the six-sided tapered crystal shape.

I'm adding gold claw spikes as a decorative setting around the cluster base, then sketching out the gold ingot stack using tapered square frustums (low-poly cylinders rotated 45°) to form trapezoidal bars.

I'm arranging the ingot stack into a pyramid shape - three in the base row, two offset above, one on top - and positioning it in the back-right corner of the floor near the existing heap lumps, nudging one lump out of the way to avoid overlap.

Now I'm designing a pearl necklace draped over the chest's front lip using a catmull-rom path that dips toward the coin spill, with pearl bead spheres strung along the curve and a gold clasp pendant holding a teardrop ruby at the lowest point.

For placement, I'm using heightAt to sample points along the x-range so the path hugs the coin surface naturally rather than floating. I'm applying the same surface-sampling trick for scattered hero gems and adding a gold torus ring with an embedded gem resting on the coins.

Now I'm working on standing coin pieces leaning against the heaps -- six large coins built from a cylinder plus two circular face planes to carry the coin texture on front and back, positioned near the front of the heap and rotated so their faces tilt toward the viewer.

The face circles need rotating about X by ±π/2 so their local +Z normal aligns with the coin's Y axis for top/bottom faces, and since the emblem is rotationally symmetric the exact UV orientation doesn't matter.

Now I'm defining a `heroCoin` helper that builds a coin from a cylinder plus two rotated face discs and a torus rim, placed relative to a frame oriented by yaw and lean, with roughly 7 hero coins scattered and a few flat ones lying face-up on top of heaps for visibility.

For the rest of the coins, I'm planning several neat stacks of 5-9 coins scattered around the floor (front-right cluster plus one on the left), using jittered cylinder discs for the stack bodies and topping each stack with a textured hero disc for the face detail. I'm skipping extra lights, and adding small sparkle glint cards at about eight key spots -- gems, crown, orb, goblet rim, coins -- each sized around 0.14.

For the coin mounds, I'm building sphere-based lump parts in gold-dark flat shading, scaled and rotated to match the pile's underlying surface normals, then feeding those lumps into the scatter surface sampler so individual coins land correctly across the mound's geometry. Each coin's orientation combines an aim quaternion toward the local surface normal, a small random tilt around a horizontal axis, and a random spin about its own vertical axis for natural-looking scatter.

Skipping embossing for simplicity. Now estimating how many coins I need by calculating the surface area of the heap, treating it roughly as a half-ellipsoid to figure out dense coverage.

I'm balancing coin size versus triangle budget: bigger coins with fewer sides (8-sided cylinders) let me use around 500 coins while keeping total triangle count under 20k, and I can skip the bottom cap on each coin since it won't be visible.

Adding up other elements — hero coins, lathed goblets, chest, crown, gems — I estimate roughly 25k triangles total, which stays within budget. I also want the dark gold base to peek through gaps between coins on the mounds, including coins scattered across the chest lump's interior top surface. For hit detection I need to confirm the Hit object exposes both position and normal accessors.

I'm defining a scatter filter that excludes coins facing downward, below a height threshold, or inside the chest's local bounding box, using an inverse transform to convert world points into chest-local coordinates for that containment check. I also want to exclude coins hidden under the crown's cushion and adjust goblet base heights to account for coin pile thickness so they don't float. For the chest's interior coin spill, I'm positioning a mound so its top rises above the rim for a convincing overflow effect.

Working out the front spill lump's position relative to the chest's front face is trickier -- I want the coins to hug the lower portion of the front plate without fully covering the emblem above, so I'm adjusting the lump's z-offset and vertical radius so it reads as spilling naturally from the rim down toward the floor.

I'll place a spill heap on the right side of the front panel, offset so it avoids the central emblem and reaches up to the rim, giving the impression of coins pouring over that edge. Now I'm finalizing the world coordinates for all the lumps, accounting for the chest's center position and its slight yaw rotation.

I'm checking lump F's extent against the chest's left edge since it overlaps slightly, so I need the exclusion filter to catch any coin poking through the chest walls, not just ones inside the interior volume.

Looking at the other heaps: G in the back-left overlaps the chest's back fine, and E's right-side heap sits near the chest's right edge with its top around y=0.32. For H in the back-right, I'm tracing where the opened lid's arch bulges backward past 90°, since it hinges at the back top and extends further back and down than the closed position would.

Checking the lid arch region above y>0.47 against lump G's top at 0.3 confirms no collision there, so that clearance works out fine. Now I'm checking whether a back-left crystal placed near G's position would sit cleanly on top of it or overlap with its base.

Moving on to ingots and goblets, I'm verifying the right-back ingot clears the E lump's footprint and sits properly on the floor. For the goblets, I'm adjusting G1's position so it rests on F's top surface instead of near a low edge, and working out G2's placement relative to the cushion and E's extended x-range.

For G3, the toppled goblet, I'm angling it to lie on its side with its mouth pointing front-right so a coin trail can spill out naturally. G4 gets shrunk slightly and nudged to sit better on the D lump's low top surface.

Now I'm positioning the coin stacks, checking S1's placement against C's footprint and the floor height, then stacking additional piles at varying heights nearby.

Mixing flat and tilted coins near z 1.45, then placing the right-side coin stacks at various heights near G2, and starting the left-side stacks with a six-coin pile around (-0.95, 0, 0.8).

For positioning, I'll use a heightAt function to set the base of each stack so it sits correctly on the floor or lump surfaces, with a slight sink for realism. I'm also adding a few hero coins leaning against the lumps at a 20° angle for visual interest.

Now I'm placing the gems themselves—ruby, sapphire, and others—scattered across the coin piles and resting on the interior pile inside the chest, using height sampling to sit them naturally on the surfaces.

I'm scattering 26 smaller gems across the lumps using a separate rng with minimum distance filtering, giving them a lathe-shaped geometry oriented to the surface normal and grouping them by seven color categories so I can add a subtle glow per color.

Now I'm moving on to writing the SVG texture for the coin face.

Still writing coin face SVG...

Drawing wing feather details...

Still writing shield and rune band SVG...

Finishing the tassel's strand fan, then sketching a hex-socket lock texture with a glowing cyan gradient and rune lines, reusing the coin face for the ingot stamp. That brings me to seven textures, so I'll skip the banner idea and move to writing the actual code along with metadata like name, description, and style.

For the implementation, I'm setting up a transform helper class and a height function for terrain lumps, flagging rotated lumps as non-solid ground so they're excluded from height calculations. I'm also working out a brilliant-cut gem geometry using a lathe profile, thinking through how the point ordering affects the normal direction when revolved around the Y axis.

Flat segments at 8 steps with spin offset for irregularity, scaling overall size by radius. I'm also defining a crystal lathe profile with six segments scaled by radius and height, then starting to write a goblet-generating function using the lathe utility.

Writing lathe outline helper...

For G1, I'm clustering five small gems inside the bowl near the rim. For G2, the bigger trophy needs silver styling with a gold band and gems, plus curved handle sweeps defined by bezier paths flaring outward from the bowl and curving back down.

For the lying goblet G3, I'm setting up a frame that aims along a tilted direction so the lathe axis follows that orientation, placing the foot near the floor with a slight upward tilt and adding rune bands that follow the frame. I'm also planning a spill of coins pouring from G3's mouth.

Writing stack-building logic...

I'm checking details like gold corner brackets, worn paint texture, and confirming the root joint setup for the hoard bones. Now I'm working out the chest front plate dimensions, positioning the straps and emblem plane relative to the body's front face so they layer correctly without clipping.

I'm checking emblem positioning against the straps and body dimensions, adjusting its height and vertical center so it doesn't overlap the rim trim near the top of the chest.

For the lock gem, I'm computing where the shield center falls in the texture's UV space and offsetting the plane accordingly, then sizing the emblem plane and setting up its placement with the texture material.

For the lid lining, I'm checking that the paint pattern picks the dominant world-axis normal correctly for the tilted lid face, then laying out a grid of gold studs at the lattice intersections across the lining surface.

I'll write a general helper to compute world transforms for frame-relative placements, then reuse it for both the lid studs and the chest strap studs. Now I'm setting up the TypeScript imports for the builder, geometry merging utilities, and frame types, making sure to only import what I actually use to avoid strict lint errors.

Still writing imports and palette setup...

Defining more paint colors...

Still writing texture functions...

Defining lump parts and surface...

Still working out coin orientation...

Now I'm grouping colors together and moving on to the height calculation and chest-building helpers, then writing the crown geometry with a domed cap and a lathed band shape.

I'm considering whether the lathed band profile needs to close properly so the inner wall doesn't flip normals and create culling issues—closing the loop by repeating the first point should fix the inward-facing segment.

Checking the remaining directions confirms the full loop traces correctly: bottom-outward, up-outside, top-inward, down-inside all give consistent normals, matching my point ordering for the ring profile. I'm now writing a small helper function that builds a LatheGeometry from an array of 2D points and a segment count.

Now I'm laying out the crown's decorative elements: gold ridge rings at the band's top and bottom (built as thin tori rotated to lie horizontally), a ring of pearls spaced around the crown, and a band of gemstones positioned radially with their orientation aligned outward from the crown's axis.

I'm also planning the spikes (alternating tall and short, each extruded from a profile), the four arches sweeping to meet at the top, and the orb with a hexagonal crystal to cap the crown, plus pearls set at the tips of the tall spikes. Now I'm defining the coordinate outline for the tall spike's profile shape.

Still defining arch geometry...

Checking the chest builder and prop naming conventions for consistency, then moving to the hero coin construction function.

Writing coin geometry layers...

Now I'm positioning the cushion frame to sit on the coin heap, calculating how much it sinks into the pile at center versus how the heap surface slopes lower toward the edges where tassels will hang.

I'm then setting up the crown frame on top of the cushion using a parented transform, and working out tassel attachment points at the cushion corners based on its half-width and half-depth dimensions.

Each tassel hangs downward from its corner anchor with a small gold cap sphere, and the cards sink slightly into the coin pile below for a natural overlap. For the cord, I'm tracing a closed Catmull-Rom curve around the cushion's rounded rectangle outline with a dozen points, giving it a gold-colored, six-sided tube shape.

Now for the pearl necklace, I'm building a smoothed path from height-sampled points and placing twenty-six pearl spheres along it, with a teardrop gem pendant (likely sapphire or ruby) set in a gold bezel at the midpoint. I need to carefully choose the necklace's path points so they drape naturally across the lumps labeled C and D without clipping through them awkwardly.

I'm also designing a gem helper function that batches all gems (both large hero pieces and small scattered ones) by color into merged geometries, so glow effects can be applied efficiently per-color rather than per-gem, keeping part counts low while supporting different cut types like brilliant facets and hexagonal crystal prisms.

Now I'm positioning the hero gems like ruby, placing each at specific x,z coordinates across the terrain lumps while computing their height offsets.

Placing citrine and a hex-cyan crystal gem nearby, plus smaller interior gems scattered on the chest pile with random tilts and a flat ground normal orientation for table-set pieces. I'm marking sparkle points on the hero gems, crown orb, crystal tips, liquid, and coins, then finally ready to write the actual file with metadata.

Writing build function...

Still building the part call and texture option, then setting up the batching infrastructure that groups geometries by key and clones/transforms them with matrices...

Writing the batch merging logic...

Setting up separate batch maps for coins, studs, gems, and crystals, each grouped by color/material key so geometries merge efficiently before rendering.

Now I'm defining low-poly sphere geometry for the pearls and sketching out the SVG path markup for the wing shapes, mirroring them for left/right sides.

Writing SVG wing paths...

Still adjusting the shield outline and gem socket placement...

Writing hex glyph patterns...

Adding the binding ring, then sketching a hex lock design with layered polygons for a gradient gem effect and glow highlights, before moving on to the coin face variant.

Now I'm working out sparkle tinting options for the cards and figuring out how to stamp the coin face onto the ingot's top surface with proper plane orientation, then shaping the ingot bars using tapered cylinder geometry rotated into a square frustum form.

I'm stacking the ingots into a pyramid: three bars side by side on the bottom layer, two nested on top, and one capping the peak, with slight yaw and random offsets for a natural pile look, painted gold, and stamping the top bar with a coin face.

Now I'm deciding which surfaces need texture planes — just the top bar and a leaning loose bar, since the lower bars are mostly covered.

For the crystal cluster, I'm positioning a base point near the terrain and defining each crystal's radius, height, tilt rotation, offset, and color, starting with a cyan crystal and a second smaller one with a different tilt.

I'm adding the remaining crystals with varying sizes and tilts — pink, cyan, and smaller accents — then plan to build them as lathe geometry, grouping them by color into batches with glow effects, and finishing with gold claw prongs angled outward around the base.

Now I'm adding a gold ring band around the base and tallying up part counts across all the treasure pieces — chest, lid, crown, goblets, and coins — to estimate the total scene complexity.

Setting up the chest frame's position and dimensions, then building the body box and gold trim pieces along the base edges.

For the rim, I realize a solid trim box would cap the whole opening, so I'm replacing it with four separate boards framing just the edges, leaving the interior open to show the body's top face and a crimson lining piece inside.

Now I'm adding corner posts that extend slightly past the body for visible caps, topped with small gold pyramid cones for decoration.

Still placing decorative elements...

Actually, skipping the hasp box since it'd overlap the emblem shield — simpler to add a glowing hextech lock gem as a plane at the shield's center instead, positioned just in front of the emblem layer to avoid z-fighting with the straps.

For the side handles, I'm adding gold iron rings using rotated tori plus backing plates.

Now I'm building the lid's arched shape generator...

Still defining arch geometry...

Adding border strips and studs, then placing the coin medallion face centered on the front panel — checking that its depth sits correctly between the lining and border strip boundaries so nothing clips.

Now I'm positioning the lip trim boxes along the lid's top and back edges to appear as gold trim when the lid swings open, then adding cylindrical hinge barrels rotated to lie along the x-axis near the lid's sides.

Next I'm placing the hero gem on the lid's front lip using the local frame transform to get its position and outward-facing orientation, picking a larger ruby with sparkle for emphasis. Then I need to add the coin heap inside the chest and finalize decorative touches before writing out the full implementation, which should run around 600 lines, then typecheck and preview it.

I'm defining the coordinate transform helpers for converting points and directions between local and world space, and setting up the goblet's cross-section profile as a sequence of radius/height pairs, then verifying the inner and outer curves don't intersect by checking that the inner wall's x-coordinate stays smaller than the outer wall's at matching heights.

Now I'm checking the wall thickness at the cavity bottom and rim, settling on faceted shading with sharp creases rather than smooth normals, then starting to position a ring of six gems around the knop section of the stem.

For the bowl, I'm wrapping a rune texture cylinder around it with UVs mapped so it reads correctly outward, keeping the gold trophy's band dark with light runes while the silver variant uses a gold-colored rune band for contrast.

Now I'm sketching out the goblet variants: G1 with gems, G2 plain with handles, G4 holding cyan liquid, and G3 toppled over spilling coins. For the spill, I'm scattering coin positions along a trail from the goblet's mouth outward, varying distance, lateral offset, and yaw randomly, with a few coins tilted upright as if stuck in the rim, while being careful to avoid overlapping clusters near the mouth.

I'm adjusting the goblet's base position and tilt so the trail doesn't overshoot onto neighboring heap features, checking how the toppled goblet's foot interacts with the existing terrain lump underneath it, and tweaking the radius of that lump so the goblet sits naturally rather than clipping through.

I'm also placing the small stacked disc elements near the goblet trail and positioning the leaning hero coins around the opposite side, checking their x/z coordinates and leaning/yaw angles so each coin rests against the pile without overlapping the other decorative trails.

Writing final code with card glow, frames, and sparkle placements...

Writing the build function...

Checking the Fill type import from context, and confirming part() accepts fill with a texture parameter typed as THREE.Texture.

I'm also figuring out the textured plane normals for flat-shaded discs, aiming direction for `put`, and setting up positioning for stacked coin discs. Now I'm writing a `heightAt` helper function to compute terrain height at a given point based on nearby ground lumps...

Writing heightAt function...

I'm also working through an `inChest` containment check using local coordinates relative to the chest's position and rotation, checking against the chest's width, depth, and rim height -- but I'm noticing the spill lump near the chest's front lip overlaps with the region meant to be "inside" the chest, so I need to reconsider the boundary condition there.

Checking that interior lumps still get included above the rim and excluded along the sides below it, then moving to a separate scattering pass for small gems on the surface with slight tilt variation, plus a scattered subset getting sparkle effects before finalizing the chest's root group.

I'm confirming the gem lathe geometry keeps triangle counts reasonable across all instances, then setting up type aliases and verifying scale options accept tuple vectors. Cleaning up unused imports and double-checking the helper functions I actually use before writing the full implementation.

Now I'm working out the cushion's rounded-rect outline with cut corners, bevel thickness, and local axis orientation using the CuF frame.

Mapping the cord path onto the cushion outline with slight scale offset for a raised look, placing tassel corners near the cushion edges, and setting up a crown frame positioned above the cushion with appropriate height offset.

For spike placement I'm aligning tall spikes with gems at the same angular positions (every π/4), checking that spike tips at radius .178 clear the inward-curving arches at radius .141 without collision given their heights.

Now I'm positioning gems on the band so they sit directly below where spikes start, confirming the vertical alignment looks correct, and working out the extrude direction for the spike geometry using normalized vectors, plus adding the crown's top orb and sparkle details before finalizing the draft code.

Once that's done, I'll run a typecheck and preview to verify everything renders properly.
